From 2028 the European Union will put a price on CO₂ emissions from heating buildings and from motor
fuels. The new emissions trading system, ETS2, was originally due to start in 2027, but this year the
EU postponed it by a year[^odklad], and Czechia and Italy are now pushing for it to be
suspended[^pozastaveni]. If ETS2 does go ahead, the state will earn new revenue from selling
allowances, which it must spend on climate and social measures[^pravidla]. Before we decide what to do
with that money, we should be clear about two things: what we want to achieve, and how we will know
that we have achieved it.

## Europe pays more and regulates more

Reducing CO₂ emissions is, in general, a sensible goal. But Europe is not alone on this path, and it
should pay close attention to how its main rivals see it. Since January 2026 the United States has not
been a party to the Paris Agreement[^pariz], and the US government has declared a “national energy
emergency” to expand domestic energy production, including oil and natural gas[^usa]. China has
extended its emissions trading system to steel, cement and aluminium, but for now it regulates only
emissions per unit of output, not their total amount. It plans to introduce absolute caps gradually
from 2027[^cina].

European firms, meanwhile, pay far more for energy than their competitors. The 2024 Draghi report on
the future of European competitiveness states that EU companies pay two to three times more for
electricity than companies in the US, and four to five times more for natural gas. It names Europe's
lack of natural resources as the main cause, but also flaws in the common energy market and high
taxes. And it warns that if Europe fails to coordinate its policies, decarbonisation risks running
contrary to competitiveness and growth[^draghi-energie].

The second problem is regulation. According to the same report, more than 60% of EU companies see it
as an obstacle to investment, and 55% of small and medium-sized enterprises name regulatory obstacles
and administrative burden as their greatest challenge[^draghi-regulace]. Between 2019 and 2024 the EU
passed around 13,000 acts, while around 3,500 laws and 2,000 resolutions were adopted at federal level
in the US[^draghi-akty]. Draghi also points out that the EU has no common methodology for measuring the
cost of regulation[^draghi-metodika]. A reliable overall figure for how much regulation adds to the
price of European products is therefore missing. Partial estimates do exist: according to a study for
the European Commission, EU legislation from 2004 to 2014 cost the chemical industry about 12% of its
value added and as much as 30% of its gross operating surplus, roughly its profit[^chemie]. The
Commission itself aims to cut firms' recurring administrative costs by €37.5 billion a year by
2029[^komise].

Part of the problem, however, is at home. In October this year the President of the European
Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, proposed a “pact against overregulation”: member states should show
which obligations come from EU law and which they have added themselves[^pakt]. Czechia has improved
as far as new laws are concerned. Since 2016 a government methodology has required directives to be
transposed in their minimal form and any additional requirement to be justified. Unjustified
gold-plating has since almost disappeared from new legislation[^kral]. It persists, however, in older
laws, in MPs' amendments and in practice[^amo-zbytky]. For example, when a building that was built and
last substantially altered before 1947 is sold or let, no energy performance certificate is needed if
both parties agree in writing[^penb]. According to an analysis by the Association for International
Affairs (AMO), however, the media and firms that prepare such assessments often keep quiet about
exemptions of this kind[^amo]. Exemptions that spare people administrative burden are welcome; people
must, however, be made aware of them. According to the Czech Chamber of Commerce, administration costs
Czech businesses around CZK 72 billion a year, and the government wants to cut this by a fifth by
2029[^hk].

At the same time, Europe has few fossil resources of its own[^draghi-zdroje]. In 2024 it imported 57%
of the energy available to it, and two thirds of these imports were oil and petroleum
products[^eurostat]. Reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels is therefore the right thing to do
regardless of the climate.

## What the indicators see and what they miss

The rules for ETS2 money have two parts. Revenue from some of the allowances goes to the Social Climate
Fund, which has at most €65 billion available for 2026 to 2032[^scf-fond]; Czechia can receive up to
CZK 50 billion from it[^scf-cr]. The state must add at least 25% of the costs of its Social Climate
Plan[^scf-25]. At most 37.5% of these costs may go to temporary direct income support for households,
so most of the money must go to measures with a lasting effect, such as building renovation, clean
heating or zero-emission transport[^scf-pravidla]. The state keeps the remaining ETS2 revenue and must
use it for climate purposes, giving priority to social impacts[^pravidla2]. Moreover, the Commission
pays out money from the Fund only if the state meets the targets of its plan, and these must include a
reduction in the number of households in energy poverty[^scf].

We calculated the impact of ETS2 on Czech households with a model that links two levels. The
macroeconomic model E3ME calculates how ETS2 changes prices and incomes across the whole economy, and
the dynamic microsimulation DASMOD carries these changes through to the budgets of 3,233 households
from household surveys, which represent 4.62 million Czech households. Unlike static estimates, which
simply apply higher prices to today's consumption, households in the model respond to changes in
prices and incomes in the way the data on their spending show. The model also tracks their savings and
debts, so it captures how a renovation is financed, and for every result we report how precisely the
data can measure it[^wp-model]. The main finding is that what energy poverty indicators record depends
as much on how they are constructed as on the policy itself[^wp-zaver].

In our scenario, the average Czech household will pay €218 a year more for energy in 2032 because of
ETS2, or 0.73% of its net income. Households heating with gas and pensioners living alone will be hit
hardest[^wp-dopady]. We compared what happens when the same €745 million over 2028 to 2032 goes to
insulation and heat pumps and, for comparison, to direct payments to households[^wp-obalka]. A direct
payment brings people relief, but an indicator that judges high energy costs by the level of spending
reads the part of the money spent on heating as a deterioration, so 87% of the relief disappears from
it[^wp-87]. The official indicators move by only fractions of a percentage point[^wp-oficialni].
Insulation and heat pumps reduce energy poverty, as measured by indicators that combine low income and
high costs, by 7.1 to 10.5%, and three years after the programme ends the reduction is still at least
5.4%[^wp-renovace].

The result also depends on how a renovation is paid for. An indicator that tracks a household's
savings as well as its income and costs records whether the household paid its co-payment from savings
or with a loan. If it draws on its savings, the indicator counts this as a deterioration: for a heat
pump, the fall in savings wipes out 36% of the improvement brought by lower bills. Conversely, the
saved part of a direct payment shows up in it as relief[^wp-uspory]. The same renovation can therefore
come out better or worse simply depending on how it was paid for. Goals and measurement rules need to
be set before the money starts to flow, and instead of a single number we should track several
indicators, each with its precision[^wp-doporuceni].

## ETS2 revenue for a more resilient economy

The revenue the state keeps from ETS2 may already be used, among other things, for renewable energy,
transmission grids and other technologies that contribute to the transition to a safe and sustainable
low-carbon economy[^ets-10-3]. These provisions do not mention nuclear power explicitly. Revenue from
the existing allowance system for industry and power generation, ETS1, has gone mainly to the State
Environmental Fund since this year. According to the Ministry of the Environment, it is to finance, for
example, new renewable sources, the modernisation of heating plants, energy savings in businesses and
buildings, and support for low- and middle-income households[^ets1]. I would apply the same logic to
ETS2, and more boldly. Most of the money from allowances should strengthen the resilience of the
economy as a whole, that is, finance our own energy sources, both nuclear and renewable, and the grids
that connect them. A smaller part should go to targeted support for the households hit hardest by ETS2.
The Draghi report, too, counts on both kinds of sources with low running costs[^draghi-jadro].

China shows that this can be done on a large scale: it is investing massively in renewables. In 2025
alone, according to the International Energy Agency, it added almost 500 gigawatts of renewable
capacity, more than 60% of global growth, including nearly 370 GW of solar and 117 GW of
wind[^cina-oze].

Such investments are expensive. For the two new units at Dukovany the state will pay the Korean
company KHNP CZK 407 billion at current prices[^khnp]. Construction is to be covered by a state loan,
which the European Commission estimates at €23 to 30 billion and has been examining in depth since
December 2025[^dukovany-komise]. In August this year the Minister of Industry, Karel Havlíček,
acknowledged that, including the cost of money, the two units will cost CZK 600 to 700
billion[^havlicek].

## What mix makes sense

In my view, the ideal mix should ease the regulations that make products unnecessarily expensive, in
Brussels and at home. The state should serve citizens and businesses, not the other way round: if it
needs certain data, it should obtain them itself rather than shifting that obligation onto households
and firms. At the same time, we need to reduce our dependence on imported fossil fuels for good. ETS2
revenue should go mainly into our own energy sources and infrastructure. The households hit hardest
by ETS2 need targeted help, ideally of a kind that lowers their bills permanently.

So what is the answer to the question we started with? We should aim for greater self-sufficiency in
energy. And we will know we have succeeded when price swings on world markets feed through to
household bills only very slightly.
